headline: New Hampshire home-care lawsuit settlement would tighten oversight for disabled residents
dek: The proposed four-year agreement would require provider-network reviews, contingency plans and a new aide directory for people who rely on the Choices for Independence Medicaid waiver.
body: New Hampshire has reached a proposed settlement in a five-year federal class-action lawsuit over whether people with disabilities and older adults can reliably receive the in-home services authorized through the state’s Choices for Independence program. The agreement would add oversight and reporting requirements for the Department of Health and Human Services, but it is not final: a federal judge must approve it before the reforms take effect. The New Hampshire Department of Justice announced the settlement in a [statement published Oct. 5](https://www.pubt.io/view/0EF56086574A0D5C5AB85B84CA1728A04B8D6676).

Choices for Independence, commonly called CFI, is a Medicaid-funded waiver designed to help people who meet a nursing-facility level of care remain in their homes and communities. The program helps participants obtain services such as personal care and other support from in-home aides. The lawsuit, Fitzmorris v. New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services, was filed in 2021 and later converted into a class action. Plaintiffs argued that staffing shortages and service gaps left some participants without the care the state had authorized, putting them at risk of institutional placement. The state agreed to the settlement without admitting wrongdoing, legal violations or liability, according to the [New Hampshire Bulletin’s account of the agreement](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/06/state-plaintiffs-agree-to-settle-lawsuit-over-nh-in-home-care-program-after-five-year-court-battle/).

The proposed agreement focuses first on measuring the gap between approved care and delivered care. DHHS would hire an independent consultant to examine the provider network, including whether there are enough workers to meet participant needs in each county. The first review would be due within 180 days after the settlement is finalized, followed by annual reviews. The settlement notice from the [Disability Rights Center–New Hampshire](https://drcnh.org/litigation/cfi-class-action-notice/) says the state would consider reimbursement-rate changes when those reviews show that the available workforce is not meeting demand.

The agreement also calls for a backup plan for every participant who is not receiving approved services. Under the terms described by the Bulletin, DHHS would identify people receiving less than half of their authorized services in a month and require the responsible case-management agency to activate a contingency plan. That provision matters because a missed aide visit can affect basic daily needs, not merely convenience. It also creates a clearer point at which the state must respond instead of treating an unresolved staffing problem as an individual household’s burden.

Provider pay is another part of the proposed remedy. DHHS would review the reimbursement methods and rates used for CFI services and ask the Legislature for inflation-related increases when the review supports them. The state would also revise its specialized-rate policy, which can provide extra payment when the ordinary rate is not attracting a worker for a particular participant. The plaintiffs’ lead counsel told the Bulletin that the special-rate process had been used only sparingly in the past. The settlement sets a framework for using it more quickly when a service gap is identified, but it does not itself guarantee a wage increase or an immediate aide for every participant.

Participants would also get new tools for finding and challenging services. The agreement would create an online directory of aides with contact information, the counties they serve and whether they are accepting new clients. DHHS would expand its grievance process to include missed services, and it would issue a compliance report every six months. Those changes are intended to make the system more transparent: a participant could see where provider capacity exists, report a failure to receive authorized care and track whether the state is meeting its obligations.

The legal timeline is still active. The [settlement notice](https://drcnh.org/litigation/cfi-class-action-notice/) says the proposed agreement would last four years and would not provide individual damages. It also says class members can object in writing by Dec. 7, 2026, or appear at a federal court hearing in Concord on Jan. 21, 2027. The Disability Rights Center and New Hampshire Legal Assistance plan public information sessions in November for people affected by the agreement. A participant who does not object does not need to file anything, but the notice says the settlement would limit separate lawsuits over the same issues during the four-year term if the court approves it.

For New Hampshire, the settlement shifts the CFI debate from whether service shortages exist to how the state will document and correct them. The DOJ says the agreement strengthens accountability; advocates say implementation will require close monitoring. The next decisive step belongs to the federal court, followed by DHHS’s first network review and the state’s response to whatever gaps that review identifies. Until approval and implementation occur, the existing CFI rules remain in place and the proposed reforms should not be treated as a guarantee of new services.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New Hampshire CFI home-care lawsuit settlement explained
seoDescription: A proposed New Hampshire settlement would add oversight, backup plans and provider transparency to the Choices for Independence home-care program.
